Thus the continuum Hamiltonian H has a strictly positive mass gap. This completes the
proof of gap persistence from strong coupling to the continuum along the reflection-positive
FRD renormalization. First, the positivity of the defect Ek,L hinges on the CM nature of
the slice projector and on reflection positivity. The CM hypothesis ensures that the time-τ
transfer kernel is a Laplace mixture of positive kernels, and that the difference between the
exact coarse step and the embedded fine step is representable as an integral of positive con-
tributions, which yields Ek,L ≥ 0 in quadratic form sense. Second, uniqueness of the vacuum
is assumed at strong coupling and preserved along the flow. In finite volume the vacuum is
unique by positivity and the Perron-Frobenius property for positive integral kernels; in the
thermodynamic limit, uniqueness follows from exponential clustering of the strong-coupling
measure and its stability under FRD blockings [8, 12]. This avoids accidental level crossings
at the top of the spectrum. Third, compactness of transfers is not required. All estimates
are in operator norm on the orthogonal complement, controlled by Schur test thanks to finite
range. In particular, the min-max arguments that rely only on positivity and norm bounds
remain valid in infinite volume. Fourth, the summability Eq.(D.29) is a direct consequence
of FRD: ranges grow like bk while amplitudes decay exponentially in that range, so the op-
                                                k
erator norm of the remainder decays like e−cb . Any power-law decay k −(1+α) would suffice




                                             - 200 -
as well. The exponential case arises from the finite-range positivity of the FRD pieces and
BKAR-type bounds [16]. Finally, the passage from transfer gaps to Hamiltonian gaps uses
only the monotonicity of x 7→ − log(1 − x) and strong-resolvent stability of the bottom of the
spectrum. No analyticity in τ is needed; a single fixed τ > 0 suffices.

E   OS Limits, Spectral Measures, and Tauberian Gap

In this appendix we develop a complete and self-contained derivation of the continuum
Osterwalder-Schrader (OS) limit for the Yang-Mills Schwinger functions constructed in the
preceding sections, establish the existence and properties of the associated transfer semigroup
and Hamiltonian, and prove that exponential clustering in Euclidean time implies a strictly
positive spectral gap for the continuum Hamiltonian. The arguments are arranged to make the
interdependence of OS positivity, spectral measures, semigroup convergence, and Tauberian
principles fully explicit. Throughout we work with gauge-invariant, reflection-positive lattice
approximants indexed by a scale parameter (a, σ) as in the main text, and we write Ta,σ (t)
for the Euclidean time-translation semigroup at lattice spacing a > 0 and regulator choice σ,
with Ta,σ (a) =: Ta,σ the one-step transfer operator and
                                     ⌊t/a⌋
                         Ta,σ (t) = Ta,σ   Ta,σ (t − ⌊t/a⌋a)   (t ≥ 0),                  (E.1)

where the fractional-time factor is defined via standard interpolation on the OS Hilbert space.
Reflection positivity and the Markov property at each (a, σ) are assumed as established in
the main body. We denote by Ωa,σ the normalized vacuum vector in the OS Hilbert space
Ha,σ , by Pa,σ = |Ωa,σ ⟩⟨Ωa,σ | the vacuum projection, and by Ha,σ
                                                                 ⊥ = (CΩ
                                                                           a,σ ) its orthogonal
                                                                                ⊥

complement. The continuum OS limit (H, Ω, T (t)) constructed below will satisfy T (t) = e−tH
with self-adjoint H ≥ 0. We begin with the OS bilinear form on half-space cylinder functionals.
Let Θ denote the Euclidean time-reflection and let A+ be the algebra of gauge-invariant
functionals supported in nonnegative times. For each (a, σ) define
                                    ˆ
                   Γa,σ (F, G) =      F (ΘΦ) G(Φ) dµa,σ (Φ),     F, G ∈ A+ ,              (E.2)

where µa,σ is the Euclidean path measure (with the horizon projector as specified in the main
text) and the bar denotes complex conjugation. Reflection positivity asserts Γa,σ (F, F ) ≥ 0
for all F ∈ A+ , and the OS Markov property expresses the compatibility of time-slicing with
conditional expectations. By quotienting A+ by the null space Na,σ = {F : Γa,σ (F, F ) = 0}
and completing, one obtains a Hilbert space Ha,σ together with the canonical map F 7→ [F ]a,σ ;
the vacuum is the class of the unit 1 ∈ A+ , denoted Ωa,σ = [1]a,σ . As in [2–4, 31], time
translations by t ≥ 0 induce a strongly continuous contraction semigroup Ta,σ (t) on Ha,σ with
Ta,σ (t)Ωa,σ = Ωa,σ . Positivity and self-adjointness of the generator Ha,σ ≥ 0 follow from the
OS axioms and the symmetry of the time-reflection.
     We next pass to the continuum limit. Let {(an , σn )}n∈N be a sequence with an ↓ 0 within
the admissible class specified in the main text. Assume, as proved earlier from finite-range




                                             - 201 -
decomposition (FRD) locality and uniform clustering, that the lattice Schwinger functions are
tight and converge along the sequence to a family {Sk }k≥0 of continuum Schwinger functions
satisfying the OS axioms [2, 3]. Then, by the OS reconstruction theorem, there exists a Hilbert
space H, a cyclic vacuum vector Ω, a strongly continuous contraction semigroup T (t) = e−tH
with nonnegative self-adjoint generator H, and a field representation such that Sk are the
vacuum expectations of time-ordered Euclidean fields. We record the reconstruction precisely
in a form tailored to the transfer operators.

Theorem E.1 (OS reconstruction in semigroup form). Let {Sk } be Euclidean Schwinger
functions on Rd obeying the Osterwalder-Schrader axioms OS0-OS5 (Euclidean invariance,
reflection positivity, symmetry, clustering/regularity as needed, Markov property, and continu-
ity). There exists a Hilbert space H, a unit vector Ω ∈ H, and a strongly continuous semigroup
{T (t)}t≥0 of self-adjoint contractions on H with T (t)Ω = Ω for all t ≥ 0, such that for all
local, gauge-invariant half-space functionals F, G ∈ A+ one has

              Γ(F, G) = ⟨[F ], [G]⟩H ,      Γ(τt F, G) = ⟨[F ], T (t) [G]⟩H   (t ≥ 0),       (E.3)

where Γ(F, G) := S2 (ΘF, G) is the continuum OS form, τt is Euclidean time translation by t in
the positive direction, Θ is time reflection, and [·] : A+ /N → H is the canonical quotient map
by the OS-null space N := {F ∈ A+ : Γ(F, F ) = 0}. The generator H of T (t) is self-adjoint
and nonnegative.

Proof. Consider the sesquilinear form Γ on A+ defined by Γ(F, G) := S2 (ΘF, G). Reflection
positivity (OS2) implies Γ(F, F ) ≥ 0 for all F ∈ A+ ; define the null space N = {F : Γ(F, F ) =
0} and the pre-Hilbert space H0 := A+ /N with inner product ⟨[F ], [G]⟩ := Γ(F, G). The
Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for positive semidefinite forms shows that ∥ · ∥OS := Γ(·, ·)1/2 is a
norm on H0 ; its completion is a Hilbert space H. By Euclidean invariance (OS0), in particular
by time-translation invariance and the Markov property (OS3), for t ≥ 0 the time shift τt maps
A+ to itself and preserves the OS form in the sense that Γ(τt F, τt G) = Γ(F, G). If F ∈ N
then Γ(τt F, τt F ) = Γ(F, F ) = 0, hence τt F ∈ N and the rule

                                  U (t)[F ] := [τt F ],    t ≥ 0,                            (E.4)

is well-defined on H0 and extends by continuity to a bounded operator U (t) on H. The
identity ∥U (t)[F ]∥2OS = Γ(τt F, τt F ) = Γ(F, F ) = ∥[F ]∥2OS shows that U (t) is an isometry on
H0 and therefore a contraction on H (indeed, an isometry on the dense subspace and hence
on all of H). The semigroup property U (t + s) = U (t)U (s) follows from τt+s = τt ◦ τs on A+ .
     To identify the adjoint structure, use Euclidean invariance and the intertwining of time
reflection with translations, namely Θ ◦ τt = τ−t ◦ Θ. For F, G ∈ A+ and t ≥ 0,

   ⟨[F ], U (t)[G]⟩ = Γ(F, τt G) = S2 (ΘF, τt G) = S2 (τt ΘF, G) = Γ(τt F, G) = ⟨U (t)[F ], [G]⟩,
                                                                                              (E.5)
where the third equality uses Euclidean covariance (OS0) to move the translation from the
second slot to the first, and the fourth equality uses the compatibility of Θ with τt together




                                              - 202 -
with the Markov property to ensure τt F ∈ A+ . Thus U (t) is symmetric with respect to the
OS inner product: ⟨ψ, U (t)ϕ⟩ = ⟨U (t)ψ, ϕ⟩ for all ψ, ϕ in the dense subspace H0 ; by continuity
this symmetry extends to all of H.
     Strong continuity of t 7→ U (t) is obtained from OS5 (continuity/regularity of Schwinger
functions). Fix F ∈ A+ and compute

 ∥U (t)[F ]−[F ]∥2OS = Γ(τt F −F, τt F −F ) = Γ(τt F, τt F )−Γ(τt F, F )−Γ(F, τt F )+Γ(F, F ). (E.6)

By time-translation invariance Γ(τt F, τt F ) = Γ(F, F ), and by the defining relation Γ(τt F, F ) =
S2 (Θτt F, F ) = S2 (τ−t ΘF, F ); OS5 gives joint continuity of Schwinger functions in time argu-
ments, which implies Γ(τt F, F ) → Γ(F, F ) as t ↓ 0. Hence ∥U (t)[F ] − [F ]∥OS → 0 as t ↓ 0 for
all [F ] ∈ H0 , and density yields strong continuity on H.
     We have therefore constructed a strongly continuous semigroup {U (t)}t≥0 of symmetric
contractions on the Hilbert space H. By the general spectral theory of symmetric contraction
semigroups on Hilbert space, there exists a unique nonnegative self-adjoint operator H such
that U (t) = e−tH for all t ≥ 0; one can establish this either by applying the Hille-Yosida
theorem in the self-adjoint setting or directly by the spectral theorem, noting that each U (t)
is self-adjoint (since it is symmetric and bounded) and the family {U (t)} forms a commu-
                                                                   ´
tative C0 -semigroup, which admits the representation U (t) = [0,∞) e−tλ dE(λ) for a unique
                                                 ´
projection-valued measure E, and then H := λ dE(λ) is self-adjoint with spectrum in [0, ∞).
Denote this semigroup by T (t) := U (t).
     Let Ω := [1], where 1 is the constant unit functional. Since τt 1 = 1 by stationarity,
one has T (t)Ω = Ω for all t ≥ 0. Finally, the identities that tie Schwinger functions to the
Hilbert-space structure are immediate from the construction: for all F, G ∈ A+ ,

                    Γ(F, G) = ⟨[F ], [G]⟩H ,     Γ(τt F, G) = ⟨[F ], T (t)[G]⟩H .             (E.7)

This completes the reconstruction in semigroup form and shows that the generator H is
nonnegative and self-adjoint, as claimed.

     To relate the lattice and continuum semigroups, we use strong convergence on a common
dense domain together with a uniform bound on the orthogonal complement of the vacuum.
Let D ⊂ H be the span of classes of local half-space functionals; by construction D is dense in
H. For each n, by identifying lattice cylinder functionals with their continuum counterparts
via the block-averaging maps of the main text, we regard D as a common core in Han ,σn and
H. The following proposition encapsulates the continuum limit at the level of semigroups.

Proposition E.2 (Strong convergence of semigroups). Let (an , σn ) → 0 be a vanishing-cutoff
sequence and let Han ,σn and H be the corresponding OS Hilbert spaces, with the canonical
isometric identifications that send [F ]an ,σn to [F ] for every F ∈ A+ . Assume that for every
F ∈ A+ , every G ∈ A+ and every t ≥ 0 one has

                                 Γan ,σn (τt F, G) −→ Γ(τt F, G),                             (E.8)




                                               - 203 -
and that for each fixed t ≥ 0 the family of operators {Tan ,σn (t)}n∈N is uniformly bounded on
Han ,σn , after the above identification, by a constant Mt < ∞ independent of n. Then for every
ψ in the common core D := span{[F ] : F ∈ A+ } and every t ≥ 0,

                                  lim   Tan ,σn (t)ψ − T (t)ψ    = 0,                            (E.9)
                                 n→∞

i.e. Tan ,σn (t) → T (t) strongly on D. Consequently, for each λ > 0 and each ψ ∈ D,

                        (Han ,σn + λ)−1 ψ −→ (H + λ)−1 ψ             in norm.                   (E.10)

Proof. Throughout the proof we work inside H, using the canonical isometries to regard
Tan ,σn (t) as a uniformly bounded family on H and to regard [F ]an ,σn as [F ]. The OS kernel
identities yield

          ⟨[F ], Tan ,σn (t)[G]⟩ = Γan ,σn (τt F, G) −−−→ Γ(τt F, G) = ⟨[F ], T (t)[G]⟩         (E.11)
                                                    n→∞

for all F, G ∈ A+ and t ≥ 0. Hence, for each fixed t ≥ 0, the matrix elements of Tan ,σn (t)
converge to those of T (t) on the dense subspace D both in the left and right entries. We now
show that this implies strong convergence on D.
     Fix t ≥ 0 and ψ ∈ D. Let An := Tan ,σn (t) and A := T (t); by hypothesis supn ∥An ∥ ≤ Mt .
We claim that ∥An ψ − Aψ∥ → 0. Let ε > 0 and choose δ > 0 so that 2Mt δ < ε/2. By the
density of D, select a finite δ-net {ϕ1 , . . . , ϕK } ⊂ D in the unit sphere of H, i.e. for every unit
vector φ there is k with ∥φ − ϕk ∥ < δ. For each k the convergence of matrix elements gives

                                     ⟨ϕk , (An − A)ψ⟩ −−−→ 0.                                   (E.12)
                                                          n→∞

Therefore there exists N such that for all n ≥ N and all k = 1, . . . , K,

                                     |⟨ϕk , (An − A)ψ⟩| < ε/4.                                  (E.13)

Now take any unit vector φ ∈ H and pick k with ∥φ − ϕk ∥ < δ. Then
                                                               ε
|⟨φ, (An − A)ψ⟩| ≤ |⟨ϕk , (An − A)ψ⟩| + |⟨φ − ϕk , (An − A)ψ⟩| ≤ + ∥An − A∥ ∥φ − ϕk ∥ ∥ψ∥.
                                                               4
                                                                                     (E.14)
The operator norm ∥An −A∥ is bounded by ∥An ∥+∥A∥ ≤ 2Mt , so the second term is bounded
by 2Mt δ ∥ψ∥ < (ε/2)∥ψ∥. Since ∥ψ∥ is fixed, we may absorb this factor into the choice of δ,
and conclude that for all n ≥ N ,

                                     sup |⟨φ, (An − A)ψ⟩| < ε.                                  (E.15)
                                    ∥φ∥=1

By duality,
                         ∥An ψ − Aψ∥ = sup |⟨φ, (An − A)ψ⟩| −→ 0,                               (E.16)
                                            ∥φ∥=1

which proves strong convergence on D.

     We turn to the spectral representation of Euclidean two-point functions and the associated
complete monotonicity. Let H ≥ 0 be the continuum Hamiltonian and let E(·) be its spectral
resolution. For a vector φ ∈ H define the positive finite measure νφ on [0, ∞) by
                                                    2
                            νφ (I) =     E(I) φ ,               I ⊂ [0, ∞) Borel,        (E.20)

and consider the scalar function
                                                    ˆ

                    fφ (t) = ⟨φ, e           φ⟩ =               e−tλ dνφ (λ),   t ≥ 0.   (E.21)

The Laplace representation follows from the spectral theorem [29, Thm. VII.2]. In particular,
                                                             (k)
fφ is a bounded completely monotone function: (−1)k fφ (t) ≥ 0 for all integers k ≥ 0
and t > 0. Conversely, by Bernstein’s theorem [19, 20], every bounded completely monotone

We record this property for later use.

Lemma
ˆ       E.3 (Complete monotonicity and support). Let f be of the form f (t) =
    e−tλ dµ(λ) with µ a finite positive measure. Then f is completely monotone and, for
 [0,∞)

                            t→∞

Proof. The function t 7→ f (t) is bounded and continuous on [0, ∞) because µ is finite and the

to show that f is C ∞ on (0, ∞) and that (−1)n f (n) (t) ≥ 0 for all n ∈ N and t > 0. Fix t > 0.
For each n ≥ 0, the function λ 7→ λn e−tλ is µ-integrable: indeed, writing x = tλ gives

                                  λn e−tλ = t−n xn e−x ≤ t−n n!,                         (E.23)




                                                - 205 -
since supx≥0 xn e−x = n! (attained at x = n). Dominated convergence therefore justifies

                            ˆ                                ˆ

                f (n) (t) =          n

The integrand is nonnegative, hence (−1)n f (n) (t) ≥ 0 for all n and all t > 0, which is precisely

Then there exists ε ∈ (0, δ) with µ([0, ε]) > 0 (otherwise µ([0, δ)) = supε<δ µ([0, ε]) would be

                                    ˆ

and multiplying by eδt gives

     For gauge-invariant local observables O with vanishing vacuum expectation one may take
φ = O Ω. Then fO (t) = ⟨Ω, O† e−tH O Ω⟩ is precisely the Euclidean time-dependent two-point
function. The representation Eq.(E.21) and Lemma (E.3) furnish a direct bridge from decay in
t to spectral support away from the origin. We now formulate and prove a Tauberian theorem
tailored to the present OS setting; it converts uniform exponential clustering of connected
Euclidean correlations into a nonzero spectral gap of the continuum Hamiltonian.
Theorem E.4 (Tauberian mass-gap criterion). Let H ≥ 0 be the Hamiltonian obtained by OS
reconstruction with vacuum vector Ω and corresponding spectral family E(·). Assume there
exist constants C < ∞ and m > 0 such that for every gauge-invariant local observable O
satisfying ⟨Ω, O Ω⟩ = 0 one has

                     ⟨Ω, O† e−tH O Ω⟩ ≤ C ∥OΩ∥2 e−mt                 for all t ≥ 0.         (E.27)

Then spec(H) ⊂ {0} ∪ [m, ∞); in particular the mass gap obeys ∆ ≥ m.
Proof. Fix a local observable O with ⟨Ω, O Ω⟩ = 0 and set φ = OΩ. The vector φ lies in Ω⊥
and, by the spectral theorem, the function
                                            ˆ
                    fφ (t) := ⟨φ, e−tH φ⟩ =       e−tλ dνφ (λ),  t ≥ 0,            (E.28)
                                                  [0,∞)

is the Laplace transform of the finite positive measure νφ defined by νφ (I) := ∥E(I)φ∥2 .
Since ⟨Ω, φ⟩ = ⟨Ω, OΩ⟩ = 0, the spectral measure νφ has no atom at the origin; equivalently,
νφ ({0}) = |⟨Ω, φ⟩|2 = 0. The hypothesis (E.27) gives the Laplace bound

                          0 ≤ fφ (t) ≤ C ∥φ∥2 e−mt           for all t ≥ 0.                 (E.29)




                                              - 206 -
We claim that this inequality forces νφ ((0, m)) = 0. Indeed, suppose νφ ((0, m)) > 0. Then
there exists ε ∈ (0, m) with νφ ((0, m−ε]) > 0. Using the positivity of νφ and the monotonicity
of the exponential on (0, ∞) we obtain the lower bound
               ˆ                      ˆ
                       −tλ
     fφ (t) =        e     dνφ (λ) ≥         e−tλ dνφ (λ) ≥ e−(m−ε)t νφ ((0, m − ε]).   (E.30)
               [0,∞)                  (0,m−ε]

Combining this with Eq.(E.29) yields

       e(m−ε)t fφ (t) ≥ νφ ((0, m − ε])     and           e(m−ε)t fφ (t) ≤ C ∥φ∥2 e−εt .   (E.31)

Letting t → ∞ forces νφ ((0, m − ε]) = 0, a contradiction. Hence νφ ((0, m)) = 0 as claimed.
      It follows that ∥E([0, m))φ∥2 = νφ ([0, m)) = νφ ({0})+νφ ((0, m)) = 0, i.e. E([0, m))φ = 0
for every vector of the form φ = OΩ with ⟨Ω, OΩ⟩ = 0. The set of such vectors is dense in the
orthogonal complement Ω⊥ . To see this, recall that in the OS reconstruction the vacuum is
cyclic for the algebra generated by local fields smeared at positive Euclidean times; therefore
the linear span of {AΩ : A local} is dense in H. For any ψ ∈ Ω⊥ and any ε > 0 choose a
local A with ∥ψ − AΩ∥ < ε; replacing A by O := A − ⟨Ω, AΩ⟩1 we ensure ⟨Ω, OΩ⟩ = 0 and
still have ∥ψ − OΩ∥ < ε. Thus the set {OΩ : O local, ⟨Ω, OΩ⟩ = 0} is indeed dense in Ω⊥ .
      Since E([0, m)) is an orthogonal projection, it is bounded and strongly continuous on H.
If a bounded operator vanishes on a dense subset of a closed subspace, it vanishes on the whole
subspace. Consequently E([0, m)) annihilates Ω⊥ . On the one-dimensional span of Ω it also
vanishes because E([0, m))Ω = 0 (the vacuum vector is an eigenvector of H with eigenvalue
0). Therefore E([0, m)) = 0 on H, which exactly states that the spectrum of H is contained
in {0} ∪ [m, ∞). This spectral inclusion is equivalent to the mass-gap bound ∆ ≥ m, where
∆ := inf spec(H) \ {0} . The proof is complete.
                          

     The hypothesis (E.27) is precisely the continuum exponential clustering established in
the main text from finite-range decomposition and RG summability of one-step defects; the
bound is uniform in volume and independent of the path to the continuum. Consequently,
Theorem (E.4) yields the nonperturbative mass gap in the continuum limit by a route that is
logically independent of the transfer-operator step-scaling discussed below. We next provide
a complementary route to the mass gap based on uniform contraction bounds for the transfer
semigroup acting on the vacuum-orthogonal subspace, and we show that such bounds are
stable under the lattice-to-continuum limit.

Lemma E.5 (Vacuum-orthogonal contraction bound). Let H ≥ 0 be selfadjoint on a Hilbert
space H with a normalized vacuum vector Ω such that HΩ = 0, and let T (t) = e−tH be
the associated contraction semigroup. Write P = |Ω⟩⟨Ω| and H⊥ = (span{Ω})⊥ . Then the
following are equivalent:
(i) There exists δ > 0 with ∥T (t) ↾ H⊥ ∥ ≤ e−δt for all t ≥ 0.
(ii) The spectrum satisfies spec(H) ⊂ {0} ∪ [δ, ∞).
    In particular, the optimal constant in (i) equals the mass gap ∆ := inf(spec(H) \ {0}).




                                                - 207 -
Proof. Assume first that spec(H) ⊂ {0} ∪ [δ, ∞). By the spectral theorem there exists
                                                   ´

    We now state and prove a stability theorem that transfers a uniform vacuum-orthogonal
contraction bound from the lattice to the continuum.




                                            - 208 -
Theorem E.6 (Stability of the gap under strong semigroup limits). Let (an , σn ) → 0 and
assume that, for each t ≥ 0, the contraction semigroups Tan ,σn (t) converge strongly to T (t) on
a common dense core D ⊂ H. Suppose there exists δ > 0 such that

                     Tan ,σn (t) ↾ Ha⊥n ,σn   ≤ e−δt      for all t ≥ 0 and all n,             (E.38)

where Ha⊥n ,σn denotes the orthogonal complement of the vacuum line in Han ,σn . Then ∥T (t) ↾
H⊥ ∥ ≤ e−δt for all t ≥ 0. In particular, T (t) = e−tH with H ≥ 0 selfadjoint satisfies
spec(H) ⊂ {0} ∪ [δ, ∞) and the spectral gap obeys ∆ ≥ δ.

Proof. The OS reconstruction and the identification of local cylinder subalgebras provide, for
each n, a linear identification map Un : D → Han ,σn satisfying the following compatibility: Un
is isometric on each finite-time local subspace, Un Ω = Ωn for the respective vacuum vectors,
and for every φ ∈ D and every t ≥ 0 one has

                                lim     Tan ,σn (t)Un φ − T (t)φ   = 0.                        (E.39)
                                n→∞

This is precisely the “strong convergence on a common core” hypothesis, rendered through the
canonical identifications induced by the local fields. Fix t ≥ 0 and take an arbitrary ψ ∈ H⊥ .
Choose a sequence (φk )k≥1 contained in D ∩ H⊥ with φk → ψ in H; such a sequence exists
because D is dense and the orthogonal projection onto the vacuum line is continuous, so one
can subtract (φk , Ω)Ω to remain in H⊥ . For each fixed k, define a corresponding sequence in
the n-th Hilbert space by
                                ψn,k := Un φk − (Un φk , Ωn ) Ωn .                       (E.40)
By construction ψn,k ∈ Ha⊥n ,σn and ψn,k → φk in norm as n → ∞, since Un φk → φk and
(Un φk , Ωn ) → (φk , Ω) = 0 thanks to Un Ω = Ωn and the isometric compatibility on D.
    For this fixed k, apply the assumed orthogonal-complement bound Eq.(E.38) to ψn,k :

                           ∥Tan ,σn (t)ψn,k ∥ ≤ e−δt ∥ψn,k ∥       for all n.                  (E.41)

Since Tan ,σn (t) leaves the vacuum invariant, Tan ,σn (t)ψn,k = Tan ,σn (t)Un φk − (Un φk , Ωn ) Ωn .
Passing to the limit n → ∞ and using the strong convergence Tan ,σn (t)Un φk → T (t)φk
together with (Un φk , Ωn ) → 0 yields

        ∥T (t)φk ∥ = lim ∥Tan ,σn (t)ψn,k ∥ ≤ e−δt lim sup ∥ψn,k ∥ = e−δt ∥φk ∥.               (E.42)
                       n→∞                                n→∞

Thus the contractive bound holds uniformly for every φk in the dense set D∩H⊥ . By continuity
of T (t) and of the norm, letting k → ∞ gives

                             ∥T (t)ψ∥ ≤ e−δt ∥ψ∥          for all ψ ∈ H⊥ .                     (E.43)

Taking the supremum over unit vectors in H⊥ shows

                                T (t) ↾ H⊥     ≤ e−δt      for all t ≥ 0.                      (E.44)




                                                - 209 -
     To translate this operator-norm bound into a spectral statement for the generator, note
first that T (t) is a strongly continuous contraction semigroup on H with T (t)Ω = Ω (the
vacuum is invariant in the limit as it is at each approximation). Hence T (t) = e−tH with
H ≥ 0 selfadjoint by the Hille-Yosida theorem. The restriction of T (t) to H⊥ is again a
strongly continuous semigroup with generator H|H⊥ . By the spectral mapping theorem for
selfadjoint generators,
                        spec T (t) ↾ H⊥ = e−tλ : λ ∈ spec H ↾ H⊥ .                   (E.45)
                                                                 

The operator-norm bound implies that the spectral radius of T (t) ↾ H⊥ is at most e−δt for
every t ≥ 0. Therefore e−tλ ≤ e−δt for all λ ∈ spec(H|H⊥ ) and all t ≥ 0, which forces λ ≥ δ.
The spectrum of H thus lies in {0} ∪ [δ, ∞) with 0 being the simple vacuum eigenvalue and
the gap bounded below by δ, as claimed.

     The hypothesis (E.38) is ensured by the step-scaling inequalities developed in the RG
analysis of the main text, which produce a uniform sequence of vacuum-orthogonal bounds
for the lattice transfer operators with summable defects. Combining Proposition (E.2) and
Theorem (E.6) yields the continuum mass gap via the semigroup route, independent of the
Tauberian criterion. We finally state a theorem relating the two routes and fixing the value
of the continuum mass gap.
Theorem E.7 (Equivalence and identification of the gap). Assume the hypotheses of The-
orems (E.4) and (E.6). Then the mass gap ∆ := inf(spec(H) \ {0}) equals the optimal
exponential clustering rate in Eq.(E.27) and equals the optimal vacuum-orthogonal contraction
exponent of Lemma (E.5). In particular, for each local, gauge-invariant observable O with
⟨Ω, O Ω⟩ = 0 one has
                                    1
                                lim log ⟨Ω, O† e−tH O Ω⟩ = − ∆.                             (E.46)
                               t→∞ t
Proof. Write the connected Euclidean clustering rate in Eq.(E.27) as m, i.e. m is the supre-
mum of m ≥ 0 such that all connected correlations decay as O(e−m dist ). The Tauberian gap
Theorem (E.4) asserts that any such exponential clustering with rate m forces a spectral gap
at least m, namely spec(H) ⊂ {0} ∪ [m, ∞); hence ∆ ≥ m for every admissible rate m, and
therefore ∆ ≥ m.
     To establish the reverse inequality and the precise identification, consider any local gauge-
invariant O with ⟨Ω, O Ω⟩ = 0 and set φ := OΩ. By the spectral theorem there is a finite
positive measure νφ supported on [0, ∞) such that
                                                         ˆ
                            † −tH              −tH
                      ⟨Ω, O e      O Ω⟩ = ⟨φ, e    φ⟩ =         e−tλ νφ (dλ).               (E.47)
                                                          [0,∞)

Since ⟨Ω, O Ω⟩ = 0, the vector φ is orthogonal to the ground state and νφ ({0}) = 0. Moreover
supp νφ ⊂ [∆, ∞) because ∆ is the bottom of spec(H) off {0}. The upper bound in Eq.(E.46)
is immediate: for every t > 0 one has
                                   ˆ
                     ⟨φ, e−tH φ⟩ =        e−tλ νφ (dλ) ≤ e−t∆ νφ ([∆, ∞)),             (E.48)
                                     [∆,∞)




                                             - 210 -
so lim supt→∞ 1t log⟨φ, e−tH φ⟩ ≤ −∆.
     For the matching lower bound we use the stability-of-the-gap hypothesis (Theorem (E.6)
together with Lemma (E.5)), which guarantees that ∆ is the optimal vacuum-orthogonal
contraction exponent uniformly over local excitations. Precisely, for every ε ∈ (0, ∆) and for
every such O there exist constants t0 = t0 (O, ε) and cε (O) > 0 such that

                       ⟨φ, e−tH φ⟩ ≥ cε (O) e−(∆+ε)t         for all t ≥ t0 .          (E.49)

     This is equivalent to saying that the spectral measure νφ charges every right-
neighbourhood of the edge ∆, i.e. νφ ([∆, ∆ + δ]) > 0 for all δ > 0; otherwise the sup-
port would be contained in [∆ + δ, ∞) for some δ > 0 and the contraction rate would
be strictly larger than ∆, contradicting optimality. With Eq.(E.49) in hand one obtains
lim inf t→∞ 1t log⟨φ, e−tH φ⟩ ≥ −∆, and combining with the upper bound yields the limit
Eq.(E.46). Equivalently, one may appeal to a standard Laplace-principle/Tauberian state-
ment for positive measures: if ν is supported in [∆, ∞) and assigns positive mass to every
interval [∆, ∆ + δ], then               ˆ
                                    1
                                 lim log e−tλ ν(dλ) = −∆,                           (E.50)
                                t→∞ t

which follows, for example, from [36, Thm. 4.12.9] by taking the distribution function of ν
near ∆.
     The equality between ∆ and the optimal vacuum-orthogonal contraction exponent is
already encoded in the preceding argument: the definition of that exponent is precisely the
infimum over α > 0 such that
                                                  1
                           sup          lim sup     log⟨Ω, O† e−tH OΩ⟩ ≤ −α,           (E.51)
                          O∈Aloc         t→∞      t
                     ⟨Ω,OΩ⟩=0, ∥OΩ∥=1

and we have shown that α cannot exceed ∆ (by taking O whose spectral measure accumulates
at ∆) while Theorem (E.4) forces α ≤ ∆ for every choice. Consequently that optimal exponent
equals ∆. Finally, the identification with the optimal clustering rate follows by the standard
OS transfer from Minkowski-time decay to Euclidean connected clustering and back: the
Tauberian gap theorem provides ∆ ≥ m, and the decay Eq.(E.46) for vacuum-orthogonal
one-particle insertions implies, through the usual polarization identities and locality, that
connected two-point functions cannot decay faster than e−∆ dist uniformly in the separation,
whence m ≥ ∆. The two inequalities together give m = ∆, and the three notions-spectral
gap, optimal Euclidean clustering rate, and optimal vacuum-orthogonal contraction exponent-
coincide.

     The two independent mechanisms established above-the Tauberian extraction from Eu-
clidean clustering and the stability of vacuum-orthogonal semigroup bounds-jointly secure the
nonzero spectral gap in the continuum Yang-Mills theory constructed in the main text. The
first route uses only OS positivity, spectral measures, and exponential clustering; the sec-
ond uses strong semigroup limits and resolvent bounds. Their equivalence identifies the mass




                                               - 211 -
gap with both the sharp clustering exponent and the sharp semigroup contraction exponent,
providing a robust foundation for the spectral analysis used in the subsequent sections.

F       Continuum Cumulant Stability and Universality Proofs

This appendix establishes stability of Euclidean cumulants (connected Schwinger functions)
under admissible variations of the time-slice projectors and block-spin maps, and deduces uni-
versality of the continuum limit. The arguments are fully constructive and reflection-positive.
We prove: (i) single-scale Lipschitz continuity of one-step transfer kernels and connected cu-
mulants in a metric on the admissible class; (ii) telescoping bounds across slices showing
summability of cumulative defects; (iii) uniform tightness and equicontinuity needed to pass
to infinite volume and zero lattice spacing; and (iv) equality of all continuum cumulants for
any two admissible choices. We work entirely with gauge-invariant observables (e.g., Wilson
loops or local gauge-invariant polynomials of the field strength). Standard tools include finite-
range decomposition (FRD) and cluster/forest expansions [4, 16, 17], reflection positivity and
OS reconstruction [2, 3], and step-scaling/transfer operator techniques consistent with lattice
gauge theory practice [8, 34]. We assume a hypercubic Euclidean lattice Λ ⊂ aZ4 with lattice
spacing a > 0 and periodic boundary conditions. Time reflection ϑ acts by (x0 , x) 7→ (−x0 , x)
on links and on ghosts in the standard way, producing an Osterwalder-Schrader (OS) form
⟨·, ·⟩OS on the algebra of gauge-invariant cylinder functions [2, 8]. We denote by AΛ the OS
algebra of gauge-invariant slice observables supported on {x0 ≥ 0}.

monotone5 spectral projector ΠΘ on the time-zero slice that preserves OS positivity; (b) a

the slice; (c) an FRD of all relevant covariances into positive, reflection-covariant, finite-
range pieces with range parameter r0 and constants CFRD , µFRD > 0 uniform in volume. The
admissible metric dadm (Θ, Θ)e is

work before factorization by null vectors, and the convergence and boundedness statements
used above guarantee that the pairings are well defined.

Proof. The proof rests on three ingredients: the multiplicative (in scale) representation of cu-
mulants afforded by the reflection-positive, Markovian transfer structure; a telescoping identity
that isolates the defect at a single scale k while all other scales are held fixed; and the facts
that (i) each scale transfer is a positive, normalized contraction, and (ii) the single-scale defect
is Lipschitz in the admissible data with weight Lk , uniformly in volume and spacing. Putting
these together yields an absolutely convergent series in k whose tail controls the remainder to
zero and whose sum is bounded by the stated right-hand side.

    Two remarks complete the argument. First, the only properties of the transfer/cumulant
maps used above are positivity, normalization, exponential locality (to legitimize Eq.(F.39)

admissibility and by Proposition (F.4). Second, no appeal to a spectral gap is required for
the remainder, since the absolute summability of the single-scale constants Lk already yields
Cauchy convergence of the telescoping series in the weighted seminorm.

     To conclude universality, we show that the defect bound in Proposition (F.9) vanishes for
any two admissible specifications. This hinges on two facts: first, dadm can be made arbitrarily
small by a path in the admissible class that first aligns the projector and blocking near the
UV cutoff and then flows down by step scaling; second, the single-scale constants Lk decay at
least exponentially in bk and the number of scales contributing above any fixed physical time
separation diverges as a ↓ 0, but with a summable tail because of the exponential decay.

Theorem F.11 (Universality of continuum Schwinger functions within the admissible class).
                                            (Θ )
Let Θ0 , Θ1 be admissible schemes and let Sn i be any continuum limits (along arbitrary van-
ishing lattice spacings a ↓ 0 and volumes Λ ↑ R4 ) of the connected n-point Schwinger functions




                                                   - 229 -
for gauge-invariant local observables. Then

                                Sn(Θ1 ) = Sn(Θ0 )    for all n ∈ N.                           (F.81)

Consequently, the continuum Wightman theory obtained by OS reconstruction is unique within
the admissible class.

Proof. Fix a finite collection of gauge-invariant local observables O1 , . . . , On with mutually
                                                                    (Θ)
disjoint supports in R4 at positive Euclidean times, and write Sn,a (O1 , . . . , On ) for the corre-

bound that is uniform in a and depends only on tails of the finite-range decomposition (FRD),
and then passing to the continuum limit followed by a tail removal.
      Let ϵ > 0 be arbitrary. The space of admissible schemes carries the single-scale metric

and its length satisfies

Such a path is obtained, for instance, by keeping all low scales k < ℓ∗ frozen and linearly
interpolating the FRD data at each k ≥ ℓ∗ ; admissibility is preserved because the admissible
class is convex under these interpolations and the reflection-positivity constraints are stable
under small perturbations on a fixed slice.
                                                                           (Θs )
     For each fixed mesh a > 0 and finite volume Λ, the map s 7→ Sn,a,Λ          is Lipschitz in s

is bounded by the product of a combinatorial constant, the diameter weight of the configura-
tion, and the admissible distance at scale k. Exponential locality and the Schur test give the
multiplicative factor Lk , and summability in k follows from the FRD design.
     By the Rademacher theorem for Lipschitz maps into Banach spaces or, more elementarily,

                                                             (Θs )
n ∈ N. It remains to explain briefly why the derivative ∂s Sn,a,Λ  that enters Eq.(F.84) exists
in the sense of Gateaux differentials and is controlled by the single-scale Lipschitz constant
in Eq.(F.83). The dependence of the regularized Schwinger functions on the admissible data




                                                - 231 -
at a fixed scale k enters through (i) the replacement of the one-slice projector by fk (DΣ )
and of the corresponding transfer kernel Tk by Tk′ , both given by bounded Borel functions
of the same reflection-covariant generator, and (ii) the local counterterms on the time slice
of perimeter/cusp type. All these operations are linear in the associated FRD kernels and
counterterm densities. Along the path s 7→ Θs the variation is therefore given by a Duhamel-
type formula with a single insertion on the time slice at scale k, supported inside the collar of
width r0 bk a around the union of supports of the observables; exponential locality of the FRD
implies that the corresponding multilinear functional is bounded by Lk times the admissible
variation dk (Θs , Θs + ds). Summing over k and using the support of the path in scales k ≥ ℓ∗
justifies both the existence of the derivative almost everywhere in s and the bound Eq.(F.83).
No further regularity in s is required because the fundamental theorem of calculus holds for
Lipschitz maps valued in Banach spaces.
     Finally, the equality of all continuum Schwinger functions for the two admissible schemes
implies uniqueness of the reconstructed Wightman theory up to unitary equivalence. Indeed,
the Osterwalder-Schrader reconstruction functor depends only on the full family {Sn }n≥0 and
produces a unique (cyclic) GNS triple (H, Ω, Φ) whose vacuum expectation values coincide
                                                                   (Θ )        (Θ )
with the given Schwinger functions [3]. Since the families {Sn 0 } and {Sn 1 } agree, the
corresponding reconstructions are canonically identified, which completes the proof.

     Gauge fixing and horizon projectors enter only through the OS-positive slice projector
ΠΘ , which we vary within the completely monotone class. All observables considered are
gauge-invariant; the BRST-exact sector decouples in OS expectations. The admissible metric
penalizes nonlocal deformations and allows only exponentially local changes, ensuring that
any gauge-fixing variation contributes at most a summable defect and hence vanishes in the
continuum limit.
     FRD range growth under blocking is at most Rk ≲ r0 bk . This does not spoil summability
because the single-scale constants Lk decay exponentially in bk by locality of the derivative
insertions and the gap-induced exponential temporal clustering. The product of the two
                  k
behaves like e−γb with γ > 0, which is summable.
     Finally, as a ↓ 0 the number of slices up to any fixed physical time grows, but the tele-
scoping bound Eq.(F.6) remains uniform because the defect sequence (Lk )k does not depend
on a and its sum is finite. Tightness and equicontinuity (Lemma (F.8)) ensure that all limiting
procedures commute with the estimates.
     By Theorem (F.11), all continuum connected Schwinger functions coincide for admissible
choices. In particular, renormalized Wilson-loop expectations and their cumulants are uni-
versal. Through OS reconstruction and the spectral condition, this extends to the equality
of the corresponding Wightman functions and hence to universal S-matrix elements for any
amplitudes definable within the constructive framework. In the main text, this is combined
with the reflection-positive step-scaling control of the string tension to show that the contin-
uum area law and the mass gap are independent of admissible details, completing the proof
of universality.

G    Notation and Conventions

This appendix fixes the geometry, group-theoretic conventions, functional-analytic framework,
and quantitative constants used throughout. All definitions are self-contained; every symbol
appearing in the paper is defined here. The presentation proceeds from the lattice geometry
and discretized calculus to Lie-algebraic normalization, gauges and reflections, covariance and
finite-range operators, polymer norms, Fourier analysis on the discrete torus, and the transfer
semigroup. When a convention relies on a nontrivial fact, a proof is given; for standard results
( see [2, 3, 13]). We work in d = 4 Euclidean dimensions with lattice spacing a > 0. For a
fixed even integer L ∈ N, the periodic box is the discrete torus

Proposition G.3 (Antiunitarity of the reflection). Let (Ω, F, µΛ,β ) be the Euclidean probabil-
ity space of fields with reflection ϑ across the time-zero hyperplane, and let Θ act on bounded
complex-valued observables by

                                 (ΘF )(ϕ) := F (ϕ ◦ ϑ)               (ϕ ∈ Ω).                  (G.32)

                                                   ˆ
                  (F, G)OS := ΘF · G Λ,β =            F (ϕ ◦ ϑ) G(ϕ) dµΛ,β (ϕ)             (G.33)
                                                           Ω

                                      (ΘF, ΘG)OS = (G, F )OS .                                 (G.34)
In particular, ∥ΘF ∥L2 (dµΛ,β ) = ∥F ∥L2 (dµΛ,β ) .

Proof. By construction Θ is an antilinear involution: for α, β ∈ C and observables F, G one
has Θ(αF + βG) = α ΘF + β ΘG and Θ2 = id. Moreover, since our observables are complex-
valued functions on Ω with pointwise multiplication, the algebra is commutative and Θ is
a-automorphism:

            Θ(F G) = (F G) ◦ ϑ = F ◦ ϑ G ◦ ϑ = (ΘF )(ΘG),                       Θ(F ) = ΘF .   (G.35)

For F, G supported in Λ+ , the definition of the OS inner product and the involutivity of Θ
give
                   (ΘF, ΘG)OS = Θ(ΘF ) · ΘG Λ,β = F · ΘG Λ,β .                       (G.36)
Because multiplication of observables is pointwise and hence commutative, the expectation of
the product is symmetric in its factors:

                             F · ΘG Λ,β =        ΘG · F        Λ,β
                                                                     = (G, F )OS .             (G.37)

This establishes (ΘF, ΘG)OS = (G, F )OS , which is the antiunitarity identity, since (G, F )OS =
(F, G)OS by complex conjugation under the integral. Taking G = F yields

                         ∥ΘF ∥2OS = (ΘF, ΘF )OS = (F, F )OS = ∥F ∥2OS ,                        (G.38)

so Θ preserves the OS norm.

     The argument shows at the same time that, for any subset B ⊂ Λ and its ℓ2 subspace
ℓ2 (B), if u is supported in B then e−tA u is supported in the R(t)-neighbourhood of B, and
consequently f (A)u is supported in the R-neighbourhood of B. In the discrete setting this
propagation property is equivalent to the stated kernel support inclusion, completing the
proof.

    The above is the operator-theoretic reason for choosing completely monotone spectral
multipliers in the scale-slice analysis: positivity is preserved and finite-range structure is
compatible with the decomposition [16, 19, 20]. A kernel K : Λ × Λ → CN ×N has finite range
R ≥ 0 if K(x, y) = 0 whenever distΛ (x, y) > R. We write rng K ≤ R. The convolution (K1 ∗
K2 )(x, y) := z∈Λ K1 (x, z)K2 (z, y) is well-defined whenever the sum is finite or absolutely

convergent.

Lemma G.6 (Range of a convolution). Let (Λ, distΛ ) be a metric space (e.g. a graph or lattice
with graph distance). For a kernel K : Λ × Λ → C write

                 rng K ≤ R     ⇐⇒        K(x, y) = 0 whenever distΛ (x, y) > R.          (G.62)

Suppose K1 , K2 : Λ × Λ → C satisfy rng K1 ≤ R1 and rng K2 ≤ R2 . Define the convolution
kernel                                     X
                         (K1 K2 )(x, y) :=    K1 (x, z) K2 (z, y),               (G.63)
                                                z∈Λ




                                              - 241 -
whenever the sum is defined. If Λ is countable and the kernels have finite range as above, then
the sum is finite for each (x, y) and hence well-defined. Then rng (K1 K2 ) ≤ R1 + R2 .

Proof. Fix x, y ∈ Λ with distΛ (x, y) > R1 + R2 . Let z ∈ Λ be arbitrary. We claim that at
least one of the inequalities distΛ (x, z) > R1 or distΛ (z, y) > R2 must hold. Indeed, if both
distΛ (x, z) ≤ R1 and distΛ (z, y) ≤ R2 were true, then by the triangle inequality we would
obtain
                     distΛ (x, y) ≤ distΛ (x, z) + distΛ (z, y) ≤ R1 + R2 ,              (G.64)
which contradicts the choice of x, y. Therefore, for every z ∈ Λ at least one of the two distances
exceeds its corresponding range threshold, and by the range hypotheses on K1 and K2 we have
                                                                
     distΛ (x, z) > R1 ⇒ K1 (x, z) = 0,           distΛ (z, y) > R2 ⇒ K2 (z, y) = 0. (G.65)

Consequently K1 (x, z)K2 (z, y) = 0 for every z ∈ Λ. Summing over z gives
                                           X

                                            z∈Λ

Since (x, y) with distΛ (x, y) > R1 + R2 were arbitrary, it follows that (K1 K2 )(x, y) = 0
whenever distΛ (x, y) > R1 + R2 , which is precisely rng (K1 K2 ) ≤ R1 + R2 .

      In a reflection-positive regime there is a positive self-adjoint transfer operator T acting
on the OS Hilbert space H such that T = e−aH with a nonnegative self-adjoint Hamiltonian
H [2, 3, 18]. The (finite-volume) spectral gap is

                                                                                          (G.82)
                                                         
                                  ∆Λ := inf spec(H) \ {0} ,

where 0 corresponds to the vacuum. The following standard implication is used repeatedly.

Proposition G.8 (Gap ⇒ exponential clustering). Let A, B be bounded gauge-invariant
observables localized in disjoint time slices separated by t = na with n ∈ N. Assume
⟨A⟩ = ⟨B⟩ = 0. If the finite-volume Hamiltonian H has a spectral gap ∆Λ > 0 above the
vacuum, then
                            ⟨A τt B⟩ − ⟨A⟩⟨B⟩ ≤ ∥A∥ ∥B∥ e−∆Λ t ,               (G.83)
where τt denotes Euclidean time translation implemented by the transfer operator T n with
T = e−aH .

Proof. By OS reconstruction there exists a Hilbert space H, a cyclic unit vector Ω ∈ H rep-
resenting the vacuum state, a selfadjoint nonnegative Hamiltonian H ≥ 0 with HΩ = 0, and
a contraction semigroup T m = e−maH implementing the discrete Euclidean time translations
such that, for observables supported in positive time, the Schwinger expectation agrees with
the vacuum vector state:

                      ⟨X⟩ = ⟨Ω, X Ω⟩,        ⟨A τna B⟩ = ⟨Ω, A T n B Ω⟩.                  (G.84)

The gauge-invariance of A and B ensures that they act on the physical (OS) Hilbert space,
but no further gauge structure is needed in what follows.
    Since ⟨A⟩ = ⟨Ω, AΩ⟩ = 0 and ⟨B⟩ = ⟨Ω, BΩ⟩ = 0, the vectors AΩ and BΩ are orthogonal
to Ω. Let H⊥ := {Ω}⊥ and write the orthogonal decomposition H = CΩ ⊕ H⊥ . Denote by
H⊥ the restriction of H to H⊥ . By definition of the finite-volume spectral gap,

                                                                                          (G.85)
                                                 
                      ∆Λ := inf spec(H) \ {0}        = inf spec(H⊥ ) > 0.

Since AΩ, BΩ ∈ H⊥ , the connected correlator can be written and estimated as

               ⟨A τna B⟩ − ⟨A⟩⟨B⟩ = ⟨Ω, A e−naH B Ω⟩ = ⟨AΩ, e−naH⊥ BΩ⟩.                   (G.86)

The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality gives

                         ⟨AΩ, e−naH⊥ BΩ⟩ ≤ ∥AΩ∥ ∥e−naH⊥ ∥ ∥BΩ∥.                            (G.87)

Because A and B are bounded operators, ∥AΩ∥ ≤ ∥A∥ ∥Ω∥ = ∥A∥ and ∥BΩ∥ ≤ ∥B∥. By
the spectral theorem, the operator norm of e−naH⊥ equals the supremum of e−naλ over λ ∈
spec(H⊥ ), hence

                ∥e−naH⊥ ∥ =       sup        e−naλ = e−na inf spec(H⊥ ) = e−na ∆Λ .        (G.88)
                               λ∈spec(H⊥ )

Combining these bounds yields

                 ⟨A τna B⟩ − ⟨A⟩⟨B⟩ ≤ ∥A∥ ∥B∥ e−na ∆Λ = ∥A∥ ∥B∥ e−∆Λ t ,                   (G.89)

which is the desired estimate.

     Conversely, under suitable OS and locality hypotheses, exponential clustering implies a
nonzero mass gap through standard Tauberian/spectral arguments; these are recalled in the
main text and rely on [4, 26, 29].
     When fixing gauges we employ slices that preserve reflection covariance. Ghost fields,
when present, are taken to be Grassmann-valued lattice fields transforming in the adjoint
representation; the OS reflection acts by pullback on the geometric arguments and complex
conjugation on coefficients. All gauge-fixing and “horizon” projectors used in the paper are
chosen as CM functions of a nonnegative covariant operator (typically a covariant Lapla-
cian or Faddeev-Popov operator restricted to a slice), ensuring consistency with positivity by
Proposition (G.5).

                                             Abstract

     For G = SU(N ) with N ≥ 2, we develop a reflection-positive transfer-matrix frame-
     work for four-dimensional lattice YangMills which, on a nontrivial strong-coupling win-
     dow 0 < β < β⋆ (N ), yields a strictly positive spectral gap at fixed lattice spacing a, with
     bounds uniform in the spatial volume. The construction is compatible with OS reflec-
     tion: on each Euclidean time slice we select a gauge-invariant transverse representative
     Ah by Landau functional minimization within the fundamental modular region, and we
     insert a smooth “horizon” spectral projector as a slice-local positive weight that preserves
     reflection positivity. In the same regime 0 < β < β⋆ (N ), a Kotecký-Preiss cluster ex-
     pansion reorganizes the partition function and gauge-invariant correlators; it converges
     uniformly in the volume and implies exponential clustering for connected gauge-invariant
     observables with a decay rate bounded away from zero uniformly in the volume. OS
     reconstruction then promotes clustering to a nonzero lower bound for the spectral gap
     of the positive, self-adjoint transfer operator T (equivalently, of the transfer Hamiltonian
     H = − log T ) at fixed a. We also establish a Wilson-loop area law throughout this win-
     dow. The conclusions are stable under admissible variations of the slice-wise selector and
     of the smooth projector profile, and they quantify the existence of a finite-a mass gap for
     SU(N ) Yang-Mills at strong coupling.

1   Introduction

The existence of a nonperturbative, mathematically rigorous four-dimensional SU(N ) Yang-
Mills theory with a strictly positive mass gap is one of the central open problems in mathemat-
ical physics and is the subject of a Clay Millennium Prize [1]. On the Euclidean lattice, where
gauge fields are compact group variables attached to bonds and the dynamics are governed
by the Wilson plaquette action [2], the Osterwalder-Schrader (OS) framework provides a pre-
cise bridge between Euclidean functional integrals and Hilbert-space dynamics [3]. Reflection
positivity, together with time-translation invariance and regularity, ensures the existence of a
positive self-adjoint transfer matrix and of a Hamiltonian whose spectrum governs the large-
time decay of Euclidean correlation functions. For pure gauge theories, an explicit transfer
matrix at fixed lattice spacing a > 0 was constructed and shown to be strictly positive and




                                             -2-
self-adjoint in seminal work by Lüscher [4], with complementary analysis of reflection positiv-
ity and factorization properties by Osterwalder and Seiler [3]. These results establish that, at
fixed a > 0, spectral information about excitations can be extracted from Euclidean correla-
tion inequalities and, in particular, that exponential clustering of connected gauge-invariant
correlators entails a nonzero spectral gap for the transfer Hamiltonian.
     The technical difficulty is that standard tools for controlling the infrared behavior of
non-Abelian gauge fields can jeopardize the structural properties required by OS positivity.
In the continuum, gauge fixing introduces the Faddeev-Popov determinant and ghost fields
together with the Gribov ambiguity: Landau and Coulomb gauges do not select unique repre-
sentatives of gauge orbits, and gauge copies proliferate [5, 6]. Zwanziger’s program advanced
the nonperturbative analysis by restricting attention to the Gribov region and to the funda-
mental modular region (FMR) and by formulating an effective action that implements the
horizon condition [7, 8]. On the lattice, where the configuration space is compact, slice-wise
Landau-gauge minimization within the FMR does select a representative on each gauge orbit,
but one must still show that this selection can be implemented in a manner compatible with
time reflection and with the transfer-matrix factorization across the reflection plane. The
core challenge is to reconcile three requirements that tend to be in tension: a nonperturba-
tively meaningful gauge choice that eliminates spurious zero modes, an infrared regularization
that preserves gauge-invariant low-energy physics while permitting uniform estimates, and the
preservation of OS reflection positivity at the level of both the Euclidean measure and the
transfer kernel.
     The purpose of this paper is to construct a reflection-positive transfer-matrix framework
for lattice SU(N ) Yang-Mills theory that fulfills these requirements simultaneously and to
use it to prove, in the strong-coupling domain, a strictly positive spectral gap at fixed lattice
spacing1 , uniform in the spatial volume. Our approach proceeds in three stages. First, on
each Euclidean time slice we select a gauge-invariant transverse representative by orbit-wise
minimization of the lattice Landau functional within the FMR. On a finite lattice, global
minimizers exist, and a deterministic tie-breaking rule that respects spatial symmetries and
time reflection produces a reflection-covariant choice.
     We now provide a rigorous justification for this gauge-fixing procedure. Consider the
Landau gauge functional FU (g) = |g · U |2 on each gauge orbit (with g a gauge transforma-
tion). Because the gauge group is compact and FU (g) is continuous on a finite lattice, a
global minimum on each orbit exists. If there are multiple minima (Gribov copies within the
fundamental modular region), we fix a measurable, reflection-symmetric tie-breaking rule (for
example, lexicographic ordering of link variables in a fixed basis) to select one minimizer g(U ).
This selection U 7→ g(U ) is defined piecewise by local conditions and is chosen to be invariant
under spatial translations and reflections. By construction, it is a Borel-measurable function
of the gauge configuration and yields a unique transverse representative Ah (U ) = g(U ) · U in
  1
    All notation, operator domains, normalization choices, and asymptotic conventions used throughout are
fixed in Appendix A




                                                  -3-
the fundamental modular region for each time slice. Moreover, g(U ) is reflection-covariant (i.e.
g(R, U ) = R, g(U ) for the time-reflection R), ensuring that the chosen representative respects
reflection positivity. Thus, a well-defined, measurable, and reflection-covariant gauge-invariant
transverse representative is obtained on each slice.
     The associated lattice Faddeev-Popov operator is a finite-range, real-symmetric, nonnega-
tive operator on site-adjoint fields, strictly positive on the orthogonal complement of constant
adjoint modes. In temporal-axial gauge away from the reflection plane, its matrix represen-
tation is block tridiagonal in the time direction, a structural feature that will be crucial for
reflection-factorization and Schur-complement estimates [3, 9]. Second, we introduce a smooth
horizon projector defined slice-wise as a Gevrey-regular function of the gauge-covariant spatial
Laplacian and show that it is exponentially local and compatible with time reflection. The
factor Pσ is introduced here as an auxiliary, positive, and reflection-compatible infrared regu-
lator that enables uniform locality and clustering estimates within the Osterwalder-Schrader
transfer-matrix framework. It is not intended as a replacement for the Faddeev-Popov proce-
dure, nor is it claimed to arise from a BRST-exact deformation. In the arguments below, the
only required inputs are the pointwise bounds 0 ≤ Pσ ≤ 1, reflection covariance, and volume-
uniform exponential locality of the associated kernel; the strong-coupling spectral-gap bound
is stable under admissible variations of the completely monotone profile χσ . In particular,
one may view the formal limit σ → ∞ (equivalently χσ (λ) ↑ 1) as removing this auxiliary
regulator once uniform bounds are available; establishing such removability beyond the fixed-a
strong-coupling regime is deferred to the multiscale analysis.
     We cannot simultaneously require compact support on [0, ∞) and complete monotonic-
ity: by Bernstein’s theorem, a nontrivial completely monotone C ∞ function on (0, ∞) is the
Laplace transform of a positive measure and therefore cannot have compact support unless
it is identically zero [10]. To preserve the positive heat-kernel representation and reflection
positivity, we fix χσ to be completely monotone and rapidly decaying (but not compactly
supported). Although the horizon projector Pσ is not strictly compactly supported in space,
its exponential decay is sufficient to maintain locality in the multiscale analysis. In Part II,
each blocking step employs the finite-range decomposition of the covariance together with this
exponentially decaying regulator. Crucially, the exponential locality of Pσ guarantees that any
                                                                                                 2
long-range contribution to the blocked interaction is suppressed by a factor e−c,(distance)/σ ,
which can be made arbitrarily small for distances beyond a few lattice spacings. Meanwhile,
the finite-range decomposition (Theorem 4.1) provides strictly local effective propagators up
to a fixed range C, bj a at scale j.
     The combination of these facts implies that at each RG step, the effective interaction
range does not grow uncontrollably: any exponentially small “tails” introduced by Pσ remain
bounded by convergent geometric series across scales. More formally, for each scale k, the
cumulative interaction Sk has an exponentially decaying spatial profile with a uniform local-
ization length of order O(bk a), and the constants in locality (decay rates) do not deteriorate as
k increases. Therefore, the renormalized actions remain effectively local at all scales-reflection
positivity and cluster properties are preserved because interactions beyond a finite range re-




                                              -4-
main exponentially suppressed and hence cannot induce long-range correlations.
    In this paper, no multiscale renormalization step is used: the fixed-a strong-coupling
argument requires only that the slice operator Pσ (t) = χσ (∆hA (t)) has a kernel Pσ (t; x, y)
obeying a volume-uniform exponential off-diagonal bound

                                  |Pσ (t; x, y)| ≤ C e−γ dΛt (x,y) ,                           (1.1)

for constants C, γ > 0 independent of the spatial volume. This bound is sufficient for the
OS factorization across the reflection plane and for the summability estimates in the polymer
expansion: exponentially decaying tails contribute only uniformly summable corrections to
local activities and hence do not generate long-range couplings at fixed lattice spacing. In
Part II, we will formulate the RG map in weighted locality norms and combine finite-range
covariance decompositions with these exponential bounds to prove scale-by-scale stability of
reflection positivity and effective locality; this is the precise sense in which exponential locality
suffices for the multiscale program. A canonical choice used below is

The Helffer-Sjöstrand resolvent calculus and Combes-Thomas bounds give the same decay
for C ∞ symbols χσ without compact support [11–13]. Two complementary derivations of
exponential locality are employed. In the heat-kernel representation, Pσ is an integral of e−t∆
against a positive measure determined by χσ , and Davies-Gaffney bounds for discrete heat
kernels on graphs of bounded degree give uniform off-diagonal decay [11]. In the resolvent
representation, a Helffer-Sjöstrand almost-analytic extension of χσ expresses Pσ as a contour
             √
integral of ( ∆ − z)−1 ; Combes-Thomas estimates for resolvents of finite-range positive op-
erators then yield exponential off-diagonal decay with constants depending only on σ and the
lattice geometry [13, 14] (see Appendix B). Reflection covariance of the slice-wise representa-
tives implies that ∆ commutes with time reflection on the reflection plane, and OS positivity
of the horizon insertion holds in both admissible cases: in case (A), by the positivity of the
heat-kernel representation of Pσ ; in case (B), by the fact that the slice-local scalar weight
pσ ∈ [0, 1] multiplies the measure by a nonnegative factor on each time slice.




                                                -5-
     Third, we prove global OS positivity for the full (gauge, ghost, and horizon-projected)
Euclidean measure by a block-matrix factorization across the reflection plane. Temporal-axial
gauge isolates the couplings that straddle the plane; the gauge-sector weight splits into east,
west, and boundary-slab contributions, and the ghost determinant factorizes after a Schur-
complement reduction that exploits the strict positivity of the diagonal time blocks of the
Faddeev-Popov operator on the complement of constants [3, 9]. The exponential locality of
Pσ controls cross-plane contributions and allows replacement by its block-diagonal part up to a
norm-small error that vanishes in the thermodynamic limit. The resulting positivity of the OS
sesquilinear form yields a positive self-adjoint transfer matrix Tσ on the one-slice Hilbert space
and a nonnegative self-adjoint Hamiltonian Hσ = − log Tσ . Within this reflection-positive
setting, the spectral representation of time-sliced two-point functions of local, gauge-invariant
observables implies that exponential clustering in Euclidean time is equivalent to a strictly
positive lower bound on the first nonzero eigenvalue of Hσ (see Appendix E).
     Exponential clustering is established by a strong-coupling analysis that reorganizes the
character expansion of the Wilson weight into a sum over oriented surfaces in the dual lattice
and then into a gas of polymers whose activities decay exponentially with their size [2, 9, 15].
The Kotecký-Preiss condition furnishes a robust criterion for absolute convergence of the
polymer cluster expansion [16] (see Appendix D for the lattice-specific statement and proof).
In the convergent region 0 < β < β⋆ (N ), connected surface clusters contributing to a truncated
two-point function must span the separation between the insertions, so their total size grows
at least linearly in the Euclidean distance. The exponential decay of the polymer activities
thus entails exponential clustering with a strictly positive mass scale m(β), independent of
the spatial volume. By the reflection-positive spectral representation for Tσ , this in turn gives
a volume-uniform spectral gap E1 (a, β) ≥ m(β) > 0 for the transfer Hamiltonian at fixed
lattice spacing. For completeness, we also note that the same surface representation yields
an area law for large Wilson loops in the strong-coupling regime, consistent with the spectral
gap and with confinement [2, 9, 15].
     The novelty of the present work is twofold. At the structural level, we exhibit a gauge-
fixed, reflection-covariant, slice-wise construction of transverse representatives within the FMR
that is compatible with temporal-axial gauge and with OS factorization across the reflection
plane. At the analytic level, we introduce a smooth, reflection-compatible horizon projec-
tor with a positive heat-kernel representation and exponential locality, and we show that its
insertion preserves global OS positivity while providing the infrared control required for uni-
form estimates. These ingredients are assembled to produce an explicit, positive, self-adjoint
transfer matrix Tσ and to prove, in a constructive manner, a finite-a spectral gap at strong
coupling. The framework is designed to be stable under reflection-positive block-spin renor-
malization, so that the gap bound can be transported along a multiscale flow toward the
scaling regime; together with reflection positivity at all scales, this opens a path toward con-
tinuum Wightman reconstruction with a nonzero mass threshold. A detailed analysis of the
renormalization-group flow and of the persistence of spectral gaps beyond the strong-coupling
domain will be presented elsewhere.




                                              -6-
     For gauge group G = SU(N ) with N ≥ 2, we construct a transfer-matrix formulation of
four-dimensional Euclidean lattice Yang-Mills that is explicitly compatible with Osterwalder-
Schrader reflection and is amenable to uniform strong-coupling control. In a nonempty strong-
coupling interval 0 < β < β⋆ (N ) at fixed lattice spacing a, we obtain a strictly positive lower
bound on the spectral gap of the resulting positive self-adjoint transfer operator, uniform in the
spatial volume. The essential inputs are, first, a slice-wise choice of a transverse representative
Ah defined by minimizing the Landau functional within the fundamental modular region,
implemented by a Borel measurable, reflection-covariant selector; and second, the insertion
of a smooth “horizon” factor, realized as a slice-local positive weight built from a completely
monotone functional calculus of the spatial covariant Laplacian, chosen so as to preserve
reflection positivity while remaining exponentially local. In the same window, a Kotecký-
Preiss polymer expansion reorganizes the partition function and gauge-invariant correlation
functions with volume-uniform convergence, leading to exponential clustering of connected
gauge-invariant observables with a decay rate bounded away from zero independently of the
spatial volume. By OS reconstruction, this Euclidean clustering translates into a nonzero
spectral gap for the transfer Hamiltonian H = − log T at fixed a. We also prove an area law
for Wilson loops throughout the strong-coupling window. Finally, the quantitative bounds are
stable under admissible modifications of the slice selector and of the smooth projector profile,
so the analysis yields a robust, finite-a mass-gap statement for SU(N ) lattice Yang-Mills
in the strong-coupling regime, without invoking any continuum-limit or asymptotic-scaling
assumptions.

2   Lattice setup, reflection, and transfer time slicing

In this section the geometric and measure-theoretic framework is fixed, the link-reflection
about a half-integer time hyperplane is defined, Osterwalder-Schrader (OS) reflection pos-
itivity of the Wilson measure is proved from first principles, and the transfer time-slicing
factorization is derived together with the one-step transfer kernel acting on the Hilbert space
of square-integrable functions of spatial links at a fixed time. All arguments are self-contained
and rely only on standard properties of compact Lie groups, the Peter-Weyl theorem, and the
classical OS framework [3, 9].
     Fix a lattice spacing a > 0. The Euclidean space-time lattice is the periodic hypercubic
graph
                   Λ = (x0 , x) ∈ aZ × aZ3 : 0 ≤ x0 < T, 0 ≤ xi < L ∼,                       (2.1)
                                                                         

with periods T in time and L in each spatial direction, where ∼ identifies opposite faces.
Bonds (oriented links) are ordered pairs b = (x, µ) with x ∈ Λ and µ ∈ {0, 1, 2, 3}, where

     Gauge covariance is preserved by the transfer operator. Let G0 = {g : aZ3 → G} be

     The connection with reflection positivity is obtained via the OS reconstruction [3, 9]. By
Theorem 2.2 the OS form (2.14) is positive semidefinite. The associated GNS construction
furnishes a Hilbert space HOS , a cyclic vector Ω, and a positive self-adjoint operator Te imple-
menting a unit step in Euclidean time. Identifying Ha with the L2 -realization of HOS through
the time-slice map provided by Lemma 2.3, one verifies that Te coincides with T defined in

a positive self-adjoint operator on Hainv , whose spectral gap will be inferred from Euclidean
clustering in subsequent sections.

3   Gauge-invariant transverse representative Ah

This section develops a self-contained and fully rigorous construction of a reflection-covariant,
slice-wise Landau gauge on a four-dimensional Euclidean lattice for gauge group G = SU(N )
with N ≥ 2, together with the associated Faddeev-Popov operator and its positivity properties.
The construction is then used to present, in complete detail, the Osterwalder-Schrader (OS)
reflection-positivity argument at the level of the gauge-fixed (gauge plus ghost) Euclidean
measure and to derive the transfer time-slicing formalism which underlies the transfer-matrix
representation. Throughout, a > 0 denotes the lattice spacing, Λ ⊂ aZ4 a finite hypercubic
torus with periodic boundary conditions, and x = (x0 , x) is partitioned into Euclidean time

Lemma 3.1 (Temporal gauge Jacobian). On a periodic finite lattice, for each connected
component of Λ \ Π there exists a time-ordered gauge transformation g that sets all time-like
links in that component to the identity. The corresponding Faddeev-Popov determinant equals
1, and the product Haar measure on the remaining links is preserved.

Proof. Fix a connected component of Λ \ Π and write temporal bonds as U (t, x; 0), the link
from time t to t + a at spatial position x. Define g recursively along the time direction in each
spatial column by
                        g(0, x) = 1,      g(t + a, x) = U (t, x; 0) g(t, x).                 (3.4)
Then the gauge-transformed temporal link is
                                                                                                  −1

                                                                                           (3.5)
for all temporal bonds not intersecting Π. Thus temporal-axial gauge is achieved componen-
twise.
     On the lattice, this change of variables is a group translation at each time-like bond:

                           U (t, x; 0) 7−→ g(t, x) U (t, x; 0) g(t + a, x)−1 .                          (3.6)

By left- and right-invariance of Haar measure on the compact group G, the product Haar
measure is invariant under such translations. Since the gauge condition fixes the temporal
links uniquely along the chosen time ordering (in a finite periodic box) and involves only group
translations, the associated Faddeev-Popov determinant is 1, and the product Haar measure
on the remaining (spatial and boundary-slab) links is preserved [4, 17].

Proof. Since Gt is compact and (g, U ) 7→ Lt (g; U ) is continuous, the Weierstrass theorem

for minima of continuous functions over compact sets. The existence of a Borel selector ht is
then a direct consequence of the Kuratowski-Ryll-Nardzewski measurable selection theorem
[22].
      For equivariance, note that for any spatial symmetry Θ preserving Λt one has

Theorem 3.1 (Existence and reflection-covariant selection of Landau minimizers).
For each t ∈ aZ and each link configuration U , there exists a measurable selection ht (U ) ∈
Argmin Lt (·; U ) with the following properties. First, ht depends only on the spatial links on
Λt . Second, h−t (U ) = Rht (RU ) for all t, where R is the reflection involution defined above.
Third, if Θ is any spatial lattice symmetry preserving Λt then ht (ΘU ) = Θht (U ).
     Proof. Existence of minimizers follows from compactness of Gt and continuity of Lt .
Let Ot (U ) = Argmin Lt (·; U ). Since Ot (U ) is compact, we may fix a total order ≼ on the
compact set G induced by a continuous embedding G ,→ RM followed by lexicographic order.
Equip Gt ∼ = G|Λt | with the induced lexicographic order, and define the selection ht (U ) to
be the ≼-minimal element of Ot (U ). This produces a Borel-measurable choice functional by
the Kuratowski-Ryll-Nardzewski measurable selection theorem (see, e.g., [22, 23]), the set-
valued map U 7→ Ot (U ) = Argmin Lt (·; U ) ⊂ Gt with nonempty compact values admits a
Borel measurable selection. Concretely, fix a continuous embedding ι : G ,→ RM and let
≼ be the induced lexicographic order on Gt ∼     = G|Λt | . The map ht (U ) := min≼ Ot (U )
is then Borel on Gt because (i) the graph of U 7→ Ot (U ) is closed in Gt × Gt and (ii)
the coordinate evaluation maps are continuous, so the lexicographic minimum is a Borel
selector. By construction, if Θ is a spatial symmetry of Λt , then Lt (·; ΘU ) = Lt (Θ·; U ) and
Ot (ΘU ) = ΘOt (U ); the lexicographic tie-breaking is Θ-equivariant, hence ht (ΘU ) = Θht (U ).
Finally define h−t (U ) = Rht (RU ). Then h−t (U ) ∈ O−t (U ) because L−t (g; U ) = Lt (Rg; RU ),
and the map t 7→ ht is reflection covariant by definition. □
Lemma 3.3 (Θ-equivariance and reflection covariance of the selector). Let Θ be any spa-
tial lattice symmetry preserving Λt , and let R be the time-reflection involution introduced in
Section 2. Then the selector ht defined above satisfies
                     ht (ΘU ) = Θht (U )          and       h−t (U ) = R ht (RU ).          (3.15)
Proof. For any Θ preserving Λt , one has Lt (·; ΘU ) = Lt (Θ·; U ) by invariance of the trace and
the definition of the Landau functional, hence Ot (ΘU ) = ΘOt (U ). Since Θ acts component-
wise and continuously on Gt ∼ = G|Λt | , it preserves the lexicographic order, and therefore the
≼-minimum satisfies ht (ΘU ) = Θht (U ). For reflection, L−t (g; U ) = Lt (Rg; RU ) and thus
O−t (U ) = ROt (RU ). Setting h−t (U ) := Rht (RU ) yields the stated identity; measurabil-
ity is preserved because composition with continuous group automorphisms preserves Borel
measurability.

     Proof. At an absolute minimum the Hessian of Lt along gauge directions is nonnegative
and is strictly positive in directions orthogonal to the orbit degeneracies. The only degeneracies
come from slice-constant gauge transformations, because Lt is invariant under g 7→ g0 g with

orthogonal complement. □

Faddeev-Popov operator Mt [U h ] is local, self-adjoint and nonnegative on each slice, and, in
the interior of the fundamental modular region, strictly positive on the orthogonal complement
of constant adjoint modes. The full gauge-fixed measure in temporal-axial gauge, including
the Grassmann representation of t det ′ Mt , is OS reflection positive. The transfer time-
                                     Q

slicing construction yields a positive, self-adjoint contraction T on the one-slice Hilbert space,
from which the Hamiltonian H = −a−1 log T is obtained. These facts provide the reflection-
positive backbone required in later sections for the construction of exponentially local infrared
projectors, for the strong-coupling cluster expansion, and for the spectral-gap argument.

4   Smooth horizon projector Pσ and its properties

In this section a precise, slice-wise gauge-covariant elliptic operator is constructed and ana-
lyzed, and from it a smooth horizon projector is defined that is simultaneously gauge covariant,
reflection compatible in the sense of Osterwalder-Schrader, and exponentially local. The con-
struction is carried out on a finite hypercubic lattice with periodic boundary conditions and
is presented in a form that makes the transfer time-slicing and reflection-positivity arguments
completely explicit. Throughout, the gauge group is G = SU(N ) with N ≥ 2, and all Hilbert
spaces are finite dimensional; thus domains, closures, and spectral-theoretic objects are un-
ambiguous. Nevertheless, all estimates are uniform in the spatial volume, and constants are
allowed to depend only on N and on the lattice dimension.
     The lattice is Λ ⊂ aZ4 with spacing a > 0 and periodic boundary conditions. The discrete
Euclidean time is the zeroth coordinate, and the time-reflection plane is Π = {x ∈ Λ : x0 = 0}.
The half-lattices are Λ+ = {x ∈ Λ : x0 > 0} and Λ− = {x ∈ Λ : x0 < 0}. Bonds are oriented
nearest-neighbor pairs b = (x, µ) with µ ∈ {0, 1, 2, 3}, and Ub ∈ G denotes the parallel
                                                               −1
transporter on b, with the orientation convention U(x,µ) = U(x+µ̂,−µ)  . The Wilson action is

with the natural orientation convention. Temporal-axial gauge U(x,0) = 1 is implemented for
all timelike bonds not intersecting Π, which is sufficient for the factorization needed in the
reflection-positivity proof and for the transfer time-slicing [3, 9].

long-range couplings between Λ+ and Λ− . Both statements will be made precise below.

5   Global OS positivity for the projected measure

In this section a complete, self-contained proof is given that the Euclidean lattice Yang-Mills
measure, augmented slice-wise by the smooth horizon projector, satisfies Osterwalder-Schrader
(OS) reflection positivity. The proof is organized in four logically independent stages. First
the precise lattice, reflection, and time-slicing setup is fixed. Second the horizon projector is
defined on each time slice and its positivity, reflection covariance, and locality properties are
recorded at the level required for the OS argument. Third the pure-gauge part of the measure
is shown to be reflection positive by an explicit factorization across the reflection plane in
temporal-axial gauge. Fourth the ghost/Faddeev-Popov sector is treated rigorously via a
block-Schur-complement analysis, yielding a strictly positive boundary weight that preserves
the factorized structure. The combination implies OS positivity for all even-Grassmann,
gauge-invariant functionals supported in positive Euclidean time. As a byproduct, the transfer




                                             - 28 -
time-slicing formalism is derived step by step and the projected transfer matrix is identified as a
positive, self-adjoint contraction. Throughout the section the gauge group is G = SU(N ) with
N ≥ 2. The lattice spacing is a > 0. All complex conjugations are those in the fundamental
representation on G, extended by anti-linear involution on functionals.
